paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Lempke was a failed attempt by residents of St. Peter, Minnesota, to hang a cigar-factory worker accused on October 13, 1882, of attempting to rape a three-year-old girl. Lempke was held in jail, tried a month later and sentenced to two and a half years in the penitentiary, a term several Minnesota papers called too light.
According to a special telegram to the St. Paul Daily Globe, Lempke, whom the Globe called "Henry Lemke," worked in the cigar factory at St. Peter. No report gives his race, age or origin.

On the morning of Friday, October 13, Lempke was accused of carrying the young daughter of Nels Wettergren, a butcher, from the yard behind his shop into a privy. A neighbor across the alley alerted the girl's mother, and when she opened the door Lempke fled toward the river. Chased by the father, the sheriff and several other men, he found his way over the river bridge cut off and hid in the mouth of a sewer below the bluff, where Sheriff Moll captured him. Dr. Merritt examined the child and found her uninjured.

The Globe's correspondent wrote that "quite an excitement ensued" and there was "some talk of hanging," but the sheriff and marshal took Lempke safely to jail. The New Ulm Weekly Review added that "a weak attempt was made to lynch the brute" that Friday night but "resulted in naught." The Morris Tribune summed up that many people of St. Peter wanted to hang him "but finally allowed him to take his trial."

Lempke was tried at St. Peter on Saturday, November 18, before Judge Baldwin, found guilty and sentenced to two and a half years in the penitentiary. On November 22 Sheriff Moll passed through St. Paul taking him to Stillwater. No report of arrests or charges against those who tried to lynch him appears in the coverage.

The story ran only in Minnesota papers, first as a St. Peter telegram in the Daily Globe on October 15 and again, word for word, the next day. The New Ulm Weekly Review gave the fullest account, calling Lempke "the brute" and "the brute in human form," and reported the lynching attempt without comment. The Morris Tribune placed its one line, which called him "the child ravisher," in a column of political notes.

After the sentence the coverage turned to its length: the Mankato Free Press wrote that "ten years would have been more in keeping with the enormity of the crime." The New Ulm Weekly Review, which had called the sentence light, later said he "might have been as seriously punished for stealing a coat" and cited the Minneapolis Journal's remark that such sentences "make people look with favor upon lynching." No paper in the coverage mentions race in connection with the case.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Henry Lempke
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd talked of hanging the accused at his capture (A1) and made 'a weak attempt' to lynch him that night while he was held in jail (A3, A4); no one was killed or injured.

The attempt to lynch Lempke failed and he was tried and sentenced in court (A3, A4, A5); no one was killed, so the episode is an attempted lynching only, and the size of the would-be lynchers is not reported.
The Daily Globe telegram (A1) and the New Ulm Weekly Review (A3) independently report the accusation, chase and capture, and both A3 and the Morris Tribune (A4) report a move to hang him.

framing.detail: The Globe ran it under 'Attempted Rape' among 'Other Criminal Matters', calling Lempke 'the villian' and noting the sheriff's safe conveyance of him to jail.

The New Ulm Weekly Review called him 'the brute' and 'the brute in human form' and later 'the beast', reporting the lynching attempt flatly and later citing the view that light sentences make people favor lynching.
The Morris Tribune and Mankato Free Press called him 'the child ravisher' and 'the brute'; the Free Press said ten years would have fit the crime.

conflicts.note: The accounts are compatible in sequence: A1 was telegraphed the next day and describes the scene at capture, while the weekly A3 reports an attempt later the same night.

record_check.dossier: No report states Lempke's race; nothing in the coverage indicates he was Black.

record_check.record: A weak lynch attempt was made the following Friday night
record_check.dossier: The incident was Friday morning, Oct. 13; 'last Friday night' in the Oct. 18 weekly is the same day, after his jailing.
Talk of hanging arose at capture, but the attempt itself came while he was held in the St. Peter jail.
The pursuers (father, sheriff, several men) made an arrest; the lynching attempt was by unnamed townspeople, not a posse.
At least four Minnesota papers (Daily Globe, New Ulm Weekly Review, Morris Tribune, Mankato Free Press), Oct. 15-Nov. 29.
Convicted at St. Peter before Judge Baldwin and sentenced to two and a half years at Stillwater.
